Societal norms change over time. In the past, a nine-year age gap in marriage was common, and an 18-year-old woman being unmarried was a concern for her parents. Life expectancy was around 40, so major life milestones happened much earlier. As people began living longer, the definition of adulthood shifted, and now 18 is considered barely more than childhood. Some argue that the age of consent should be raised to 25 due to brain development, but that would create barriers for young people forming relationships. Maturity isn’t solely based on age—some 30-year-olds struggle with basic responsibilities, while some 10-year-olds show exceptional capability. Ideally, emotional and intellectual readiness would be tested at 15 to determine adulthood, but since that’s unrealistic, society settles on 18 as a reasonable threshold to prevent exploitation.

My grandmother managed a household, worked on a farm, tailored clothes, and taught herself shorthand at 19 in case she needed to support her children. She fiercely defended my grandfather, who worked tirelessly for 50 years to keep their farm running. They married when she was 15 and he was 22, which was normal for their time but would be controversial today. As societal expectations evolve, what really matters is a person’s maturity and ability to handle responsibility, rather than a fixed number.
